subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND CRIMINAL CODE IN CONSEQUENCE THEREOF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to tell the minister that I am pleased about the general contents of Bill C-38. It is somewhat rare to have unanimity in the House about a bill. I therefore hope that the information given to the public by the press will be objective, and that the Canadian people will understand the importance of the subject covered by the bill and, in general, cooperate so that this legislation may be applied with good results.
The bill aims at protecting our fisheries, at protecting the fish resources against poachers, especially professional poachers. There are some in all areas of the country. There are also a few small-time poachers, but they do not cause as much damage as those covered by this bill. There are also the polluters, those who use all sorts of chemicals in their industries and who do not care about the effects of the products used during manufacture. In my opinion, this legislation will invite them to be more cautious in the use of chemicals and more concerned about the damage that this waste material can cause.
There are also the destructors of the environment. They are not mentioned in the bill, but I think that the minister could examine this question. I refer to the polluters who damaged the environment by an inconsiderate destruction of our forests along our rivers or around our lakes. I have often witnessed destruction caused by the development of our forest resources, and even though this development provides employment for workers, it has disastrous consequences for the local environment: the fish disappear.
These are all matters that we should consider seriously. I remember, Mr. Speaker, when spring came when I was a child, we could witness nature's awakening and it was marvelous. On my parents' farm, there was a beautiful river which flowed into Lac-a-la-Truite. There were a great many lakes in my area and I used to accompany my parents, my older brothers and my friends on fishing expeditions: never would we come back with an empty bag; in fact, we always came back with large quantities of fish, while abiding by the laws, and it was interesting. Mr. Speaker, I remember that when, as a boy, I would go and get the cows, I always brought my fishing rod and tried my luck along the riverbank, so that there were always four or five fine trouts for my mother. She liked them very much and ate them with great appetite, and I knew this was one of the greatest pleasures I could give her. Last year, I went back to that area; again I tried my luck casting my line in these creeks and rivers, to no avail. There is nothing, not a single fish left in Lac-a-la-Truite or anywhere else. I realize that the company which operates the asbestos mines in those areas had to do it. They emptied the lake which is called Black Lake. There were natural resources there and the largest deposits of asbestos are under the lake. But, in developing that natural resource, they completely destroyed the environment: lake Williams, Black Lake, Lac-a-la-Truite, all rivers and brooks. There is nothing left now because at that time the necessary measures were not taken to protect the environment.

It is as a result of intense industrial development that our rivers, our lakes, our brooks were gradually emptied out and that we have seen at the same time enormous social benefits disappear. Our children could not only enjoy during their leisure time the beauty of nature, but also learn what nature is exactly. They could spend hours fishing, those were healthy leasure times which did not cost much to society but were very rewarding. Today when we say to our children: Go walk in the forest, go fishing. Their reply is: "There is nothing anymore, you fished everything out, you massacred everything." They blame us, and rightly so.
Over the weekend, Saturday to be precise, I went with the chairman of the Montmagny-l'Islet Rod and Gun Club, despite the bitter cold, to visit the "big lock" as it is called in the area, in the beautiful nearby municipality of Cap Saint-Ignace. The lock was built through grants from the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Significant amounts were invested twice to build a dam to regulate the river and provide a shelter for fish and give local people in Montmagny and other towns a recreational forest area. I was disappointed to note that although the lock was very well built, the force of water at high levels caused it to flow around the dam, so that large basin has now disappeared. This is a very unfortunate, because there was a lot of fish, and the scenery was beautiful for canoeing. I promised the chairman of the Montmagny-I'Is-Iet Rod and Gun club I would raise the matter at the first opportunity, and call this to the attention of the Minister of Fisheries and Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), so that funds can be allotted to repair the damage and restore that beautiful area. It is a real asset, a real encouragement to protect the environment, forests and wildlife.
I therefore welcome this opportunity, and I hope that the legislation can really open the door to a renewed effort to give better protection and get the people involved so that we may leave healthy environment to the next generation.
Yesterday, I also attended a maypole ceremony which, in our area, and probably everywhere else, consists in planting a tree to mark the end of an organization, of a series of meetings on a topic which may have been studied over a period of weeks. There again, this ceremony was held thanks to an assistance program.
Mr. Speaker, some may tell me that I insist too much on that program but I do so precisely because it gave such good results in my area that I want to talk about it and say to the government how much I appreciated it. Hundreds of young people, especially, attended that ceremony and I took advantage of it to point out to those youths how precious that tree, and the forest are to us; close by there flows a river towards the south. I also took that opportunity to invite the young, the whole population, to get together and see to it that the river, which has been polluted over the years, is cleaned up and become once again interesting, one in which nice fish may live again.
Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that last Thursday a 13-year old boy happened to spot a big 29-inch trout struggling to get free of the mud on the river bank. Then, coura-
May 16, 1977

geously, the little boy jumped in the river to get that 29-inch trout weighing seven or eight pounds and whose photo was published in the local paper. 1 have congratulated the little boy for his courage. He learned how to protect the environment, the fish and it is a fearless act that deserves to be mentioned.
Mr. Speaker, for all those reasons, I entirely support the fast passage of that legislation and then 1 hope that the regulations will be rational and known to the public. If we want the public to comply with regulations, those must be known because if they are not, they cannot be respected and we are not encouraged to cooperate. Those regulations should be well known to the public. I also wish that the department responsible for enforcing that legislation will apply it courageously not only to the weak who will fail to comply but also to the powerful. There should not be two standards of justice, there should be just one justice, one standard and the legislation should be applied strictly to big corporations that do not comply with regulations and laws. We should be as zealous as regards big corporations as we have been and will continue to be toward the weak. And the minister can be sure of one thing: he will have any co-operation and I will not intervene needlessly if I sincerely believe the legislation is properly applied, no matter the punishments or the fines that will be imposed. It will be in the public interest and 1 shall be pleased about it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND CRIMINAL CODE IN CONSEQUENCE THEREOF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to be able to participate in the second reading debate on Bill C-38 to amend the Fisheries Act, and to support my hon. friend from South Shore (Mr. Crouse) in his excellent suggestions drawing attention to some of the inequities which exist in some parts of the bill. However, he supported the principle of the bill, as have all my hon. friends who have spoken thus far.
It is obvious that the Fisheries Act needs revision. 1 am not too sure we should not be more concerned about the extensive powers of search and seizure given fisheries officers, because we have to keep in mind our fishermen, the extensive search powers of pollution inspectors, the possibility that conflict could arise over anti-pollution measures, and the possible conflict, constitutionally, with the provinces over anti-pollution measures. But I am sure that when the bill is sent to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry we can go into detail and correct any clauses which need correcting with the support of the minister.
The item I want to deal with has to do with clause 12 dealing with the catching of Atlantic salmon in sports rivers. It brings into focus measures to be taken to prevent the poaching of our rivers. I was glad to hear the minister tell us he needs to strengthen the capability to protect against the abuse of these resources. He is even going to the extent of confiscating gear and increasing fines dramatically. He mentioned the problems they are having in the province of New Brunswick, and I can tell the minister that those problems are being duplicated in
Fisheries
Newfoundland, the province I represent. Poaching is becoming increasingly a threat to the preservation of our salmon rivers.
The minister should direct his attention to the number of guardians hired, as well as to the number of man-hours and man-months provided for fisheries guardians who are taken on in the summer months during the salmon season. I say, with the greatest respect, that the government is being completely unrealistic in the measures it takes to prevent poaching when, on the one hand, many millions of dollars are spent in studies and meetings, decisions are made on man-hours and budgeting, restrictions are placed on quotas to help conserve our stocks to support the future of the industry-and I commend the minister for the action he has taken in a patient and progressive way in trying to protect the industry in years to come, an industry that could be the greatest industry in the country-while, on the other hand, completely ignoring the need to build up our guardian strength, giving as a lame excuse the lack of funds.
Each year the government keeps reducing the number of guardians and the number of man-hours or man-months. For example, last year the salmon season lasted from May 24 to December 15-and I presume it will be the same this year- but the number of man-hours allocated only allowed for guardians to patrol the rivers for 12 weeks, leaving many rivers unattended for most of the salmon season, which is contrary to the objective of river guardians.
What does this situation invite, Mr. Speaker? It invites poachers to have a field day-in fact, to have several field days. They can poach to their heart's content and literally rape our beautiful rivers, which are the wonderment of sports fishermen who in most cases are dedicatedly objective to the protection of our rivers and who I am sure will be happy with the amendments we are debating today to the bill.
What I find strange, Mr. Speaker, is that while the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) does not have the funds to keep the guardians on for the whole of the season, but has to lay them off in a good many cases after 12 weeks, his colleague, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen), can continue to pay the same personnel the greater portion of their salary for doing nothing for another 39 weeks. On the other hand, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration has programs, such as the on the job training programs which allow an employer to train personnel-and 1 do not think the minister's department is excluded-and obtain 75 per cent of their salary. 1 can only suggest that the minister apply to his colleague for such a program so that he is able to protect our rivers by building up the strength of the guardians.
The minister must recognize the seriousness of the potential destruction of our salmon stocks. The government is inviting poaching because it lacks realism. subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO EXEMPT MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS FROM LEVY OF FEDERAL SALES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on the motion proposed by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). Municipalities in Canada are facing severe financial difficulties in spite of rigorous austerity measures on their part. Mayor Dan Munroe of Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, president of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, has said that the municipal level of government could disappear from Canada in five years unless there is increased financial support from the federal government and the provinces. Mr. Munroe said, further, that property taxes cannot be expected to continue to pay for all municipal services. The situation facing many municipalities is
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
so serious that Mr. Munroe was prompted to say on their behalf:
We don't have money even for basic services now. I don't think the importance of our problem is being recognized at other levels.
That is a direct quote from the Ottawa Citizen of December 13, 1976. Recent increases in the consumer price index are especially distressing in the context of this motion, when we realize that such an index reflects increases in municipal tax rates. Another increase in municipal tax rates is likely because of rising costs in local government, so the Canadian citizen faces yet another inflationary blow to the power of the dollar. Municipal tax rate increases are reflected directly in the consumer price index.
Municipal taxes form 2.8513 per cent of the expenditure basket upon which the consumer price index is based. As a result, a 10 per cent increase in municipal taxes adds nearly one-third of 1 per cent to the rate of inflation. The impact of municipal tax changes to the consumer price index is nearly as great as the impact of changes in the mortgage interest rate. There is a great hue and cry by the financial community, and in newspaper editorials, when mortgage rates change. But who takes up the cry when hundreds of small and large towns must raise taxes to cover rising costs?
The gravity of this increased financial burden at the local level can be seen in the extreme pressure it places on people with fixed incomes who have spent their lives paying for houses as a retirement investment, only to find that increasing property taxes are turning their retirement dreams into nightmares.
One of the most challenging problems facing Canada today is that in ten years the senior citizen section of our nation will double in population. It is imperative that we do something positive to keep people independent and in their homes as long as possible. We simply cannot construct homes for the aged to cope with this increase. Then, too, the great human benefits that come to our citizens when they can remain independent of assistance as long as possible are part of a quality of life in Canada which we all seek. The removal of this property tax burden is part of the answer to this problem.
The anti-inflation white paper contained a commitment by the federal government to reassess the costs to the economy of its programs, rules and regulations. Surely, this tax by one level of government on another represents a cost to the Canadian economy, not to mention the fact that such a situation runs contrary to the basic principle of common law that the Crown should not tax itself.
As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Vegreville and others, much attention is paid to municipalities as centres of Canadian life and generators of employment. Funds saved by municipalities by the removal of the tax burden in question could be valuable sources of financing for programs at the local level or, better still, for decreased taxes. Instead of a circular type of financing in which we tax local governments to generate funds for the federal government and then see Ottawa use that money in programs such as Canada Works or, as it is commonly known, "Liberal works" which are imple-
May 16, 1977

merited back at the local level, would we not serve the Canadian economy better if we left this money with local authorities?
In this say Canadians would gain money previously spent on administration, collection and other areas of red tape. As well, more of the responsibility for local problems would be in the hands of municipal governments which are closest to the people and can respond to local situations. My experience with local municipalities is that they know best what their people need. It is not always what provincial or federal authorities deem to be in their best interests. Municipalities in Canada face numerous difficulties of administration as they try to sift through the complex of exemptions and inclusions which appear in the Excise Tax Act.
Water treatment plants have now been made exempt under the act, but certain equipment is taxable. In a water treatment plant, a pipe on one side of a wall may be taxable, but the same pipe can be exempt from taxation if it is connected on the other side of the same wall. As I have said in this House before, if the sales tax was removed from electrical supplies, as it has been with water treatment equipment, just think what it could mean to subdivision costs, thereby lessening the cost of new home building. When a bridge is built, the guard rails on it are exempt from taxation. However, the materials used in the road leading up to the bridge, including its guard rails, are not exempt.
A day-care centre, if properly registered with the Department of National Revenue, still pays federal sales tax on equipment which it purchases, but receives a rebate for such moneys. The effect of this situation is to force a municipality the size of Ottawa-Carleton to add two additional accountants to its payroll in order to administer the bookkeeping necessary to claim a rebate.
Municipal fire department buildings are taxed, but fire hoses and couplings are not. A municipality which runs its own printing service will find that materials used in that operation are taxed on the basis that such printing service is in competition with local private printing businesses. This is a fair and logical situation. However, municipalities' building and maintenance of road and water services is not done in competition with other businesses, and yet taxes are still levied on the purchase of equipment necessary for those projects. If we apply the rationale which seems to be involved in the Excise Tax Act and its provisions, perhaps the government should consider taxing the Post Office since it operates in competition with private courier services.
The complicated nature of the Excise Tax Act means that much unnecessary time is spent by municipalities separating potential purchase items according to whether they are exempt from federal sales tax as well as on the actual paperwork for the taxes themselves. These administrative costs can present a substantial burden in time and payroll to Canadian municipalities, especially smaller communities. The whole matter of preparing bids for capital expenditures is greatly complicated by this maze of exemptions and non-exemptions.
Excise Tax Act
The increased cost for this "sheep and goats" situation can only be financed by municipalities through an increase in property taxes which, as has been mentioned, is a shrinking source of funds and causes great hardship for people on fixed incomes. If a municipality is forced to borrow in order to finance capital expenditures made more expensive by federal sales tax, such loans are only available at rates higher than those which the federal government can borrow.
In one department of one municipality alone, the savings which would accrue from the exemption of municipal governments from federal sales tax is very significant. In the transport and works department of the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton, the withdrawal of federal sales tax would lead to a saving of $450,000 on the 1977 budget. As well, similar exemptions applied to the 1977 construction program would gain an additional $250,000. Thus, Mr. Speaker, one department of one municipality in Canada would realize $700,000 from the exemption of federal sales tax-money which could serve the needs of Canadians in their local communities.
The duplication of services and double taxation is all the more distressing in the inflationary times which Canada faces today. The Globe and Mail of May 11 reports the former auditor general, Maxwell Henderson, referring to the $45 billion budget the federal government brought in this year, as saying:
That $45 billion is fuelling the fires of inflation, and we should cut spending by 10 per cent each year until it's cut in half to $22 billion-it's feasible.
If the federal government spending could be cut by one-half, why is it necessary to tax Canadian municipalities in their efforts to provide services to their citizens? In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct the attention of the House to the words of Jules Renard, a Frenchman of letters and former mayor of Chaumot. Renard said:
I know at last what distinguishes man from animals: financial worries.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Fleming (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO EXEMPT MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS FROM LEVY OF FEDERAL SALES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to talk on this very worth-while motion, even though I have some problems with it. I come from a large suburban riding and I am aware of the tremendous problems that face municipal taxpayers as a result of the increased costs faced by municipalities which they have had to pass along to taxpayers.
Without reflecting in any way on the riding of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), if there is a burden faced by small communities, and special arguments can be made for exemption of equipment and materials they buy under the Excise Tax Act, then certainly there are different but equally important arguments for huge metropolitan areas with dense populations. These and other factors make it worth while considering the merits of the motion.

May 16, 1977
Excise Tax Act
At the outset I want to recognize that the motion does not, in principle, call for something new in the sense that the Excise Tax Act currently exempts from federal sales tax a comprehensive list of articles and materials sold to or imported by municipalities for their own use and not for resale. Included in the list are exemptions of which some hon. members may not be aware, such as goods for use in water distribution, sewage or drainage systems, materials and machinery used in the construction of municipal incinerators, culverts, equipment at a price in excess of $500 per unit specially designed for use directly for road-making, road-cleaning or firefighting, but not including automobiles or ordinary motor trucks, fire hose, including couplings and nozzles. Only in the last year or so have couplings been perfected by researchers and scientists.
I am sure the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine), who is very interested in research and development in Canada, will be glad to know that there has been designed what is called a "unisexual" coupling for fire hoses. This is terribly important when there is a fire and experts move quickly to put together the hoses to reach the source of the fire and put it out. Certainly, it is going to be terribly important in fighting forest fires. Exempt, also, are fire truck chassis for the permanent attachment thereon of firefighting equipment for use directly in firefighting.
It can be seen from the long list of exemptions that there are some allowances in this area now, and that they relate especially to where municipal governments have very serious responsibilities. They must spend money to do these things in order to protect their citizens. The government of Canada has recognized this and has allowed forgiveness in a number of areas. Federal sales tax also has been removed from larger trucks and most types of construction equipment. Consequently, municipal purchases of most garbage-handling equipment, and virtually all major road construction equipment, are currently exempt from federal sales tax. Certified public hospitals are not required to pay federal sales tax on any of their purchases, and libraries and schools are exempt from federal sales tax on most of their purchases. In addition, municipalities are also exempt from payment of the 10-cent per gallon special excise tax on gasoline.
Whatever else comes out of this debate, and whatever conclusions are reached, it cannot be argued that the federal government has not already gone a very long way to try to understand the problems of municipalities and the burdens on municipal taxpayers. Even though the government has its obligations, it has tried to collect revenues in order to meet its commitments and responsibilities under the constitution and has made a real effort to co-operate with municipalities in essential areas.
The primary justification for providing federal sales tax exemptions for municipalities arises from a desire to provide indirect financial assistance to local governments. Municipalities fall under the legislative jurisdiction of the provinces and it is always difficult for the federal government to come directly to their financial assistance. Indirect financial help through sales tax exemptions is one way of achieving this result. I

suspect that this amount of money is very significant to them, and I should like to go into some detail of the dollars and cents involved.
I might also point out that the federal government has taken important initiatives which are of indirect financial assistance to municipalities. For example, a decision by the federal government in 1973 to include the school-purpose portion of municipal property taxes in the formula for calculating federal equalization payments results in an annual payment of approximately $225 million to the provinces. This money is passed to the provinces unconditionally and would be of indirect benefit to the municipalities. Another important federal program which indirectly would ease the burden on municipalities is the funding by the federal government of 50 per cent of the cost of certain secondary education programs. Fifty cents out of every dollar spent on post-secondary education, of course, for some time was applied to the provinces from moneys garnered by the federal government.
The hon. member for Vegreville will also be aware that the federal government provides significant funding for the operation of hospitals and the financing of medicare programs. These contributions are of significant indirect financial benefit to the municipalities. This cannot be done directly under the constitution.
Each year, municipalities press vigorously for further sales tax exemptions. In this regard, some of the exemptions they now have are opposed by private contractors who claim that they face unfair competition from municipalities using tax-exempt equipment. Their concern was especially evident prior to the government's decision to remove federal sales tax from most construction and transportation equipment. I am sure some hon. members remember that battle royal.
The matter of equity for those small contractors is one of concern in a constituency like mine. A great many new Canadians work for those small firms-not the big wealthy operations-who count on being able to have access to and tender for municipal contracts. They would certainly be at a disadvantage if the motion before us were successful.
It is also worth noting that the federal government does not itself have an exemption under the Excise Tax Act with respect to any of its purchases. Also, the provinces, which are much more closely related to the municipalities than is the federal government, are much less generous than is the federal government in providing exemptions from provincial sales taxes for municipal purchases.
A matter which is perhaps more significant is that the present objective of the federal government and several of the provinces is to move to a system of reciprocal taxation for accommodating taxes in the area of intergovernmental taxation. That is a pretty complicated phrase. Let me try to explain it. Under this system, the federal government would pay provincial sales taxes on all taxable purchases from a given province and the provincial government would pay federal taxes on their taxable purchases. Any move to enlarge the list
May 16, 1977

of exemptions from federal sales taxes on municipal purchases would, therefore, be contrary to that general objective toward which we are now working.
Finally, it should be emphasized that many municipal purchases are currently exempt from federal sales tax. The major categories of goods purchased by municipalities which are presently subject to federal sales tax include construction materials, taxed at the reduced rate of 5 per cent, automobiles, office furniture and equipment. If additional sales tax relief were to be provided to the municipalities, this would result in significant loss of revenue which would have to be made up from tax increases in other areas. Therefore, it would be a matter of giving with one hand and taking back with the other.
Let me say that as a member of parliament I am frustrated when constituents complain to me about their municipal taxes since I, as a federal representative, have no direct control over the level of municipal taxation. The federal government provides hundreds of millions of dollars worth of grants to assist provinces and municipalities, but finds that officials of lower levels of government do not feel as great a responsibility with respect to the spending of funds as members at the federal level. Officials at lower levels are not directly responsible for the raising of money; hence they do not feel such a great responsibility in spending it. By being able to acquire grants and other assistance from the federal government, they have ready access to money for which they have not had to impose direct taxes on the public.
Although the hon. member's proposal has merit, it would be difficult to argue that the federal government has not been generous. It has recognized need and backed that recognition with indirect payments made in a number of ways to relieve the burden of costs for equipment and materials which must be borne by municipalities. As well, the government's responsibility in spending is restricted to the spending of those moneys over which under the constitution it has direct powers, these being moneys with respect to the collection and spending of which the government is answerable to the electorate.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION TO EXEMPT MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENTS FROM LEVY OF FEDERAL SALES TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention in the debate on the excellent motion proposed by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) will be brief. Speaking as a former municipal official, I am aware how frustrated municipal governments are and what problems they encounter in their attempts to raise money through taxation. The municipal government is government closest to the people and also the first to bear the brunt of taxpayers' criticism. The provincial government is somewhat more remote from the taxpayer. We, in these hallowed halls of the so-called highest level of government, are even further removed. We can impose taxes and the people can yell, but because we are so far removed from them there is little they can do.
I served on a municipal council for 31 years. For 26 years I served as reeve of a small municipality. I also served for many years on provincial organizations such as the Ontario mayors and reeves association and, latterly, on the association of municipalities of Ontario. Time and again, when resolutions would come before that association it was resolved that the
Excise Tax Act
request supported by the municipal organization requesting the discontinuance of federal sales tax on municipal purchases should be forwarded to the federal government.
I note the comments of my colleague from Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott). The savings she mentioned would come to a staggering amount in a city the size of Ottawa. She suggested, I think, that if the motion were adopted it would enable the city of Ottawa to save close to half a million dollars in one month alone. The money which could be saved in a large metropolitan centre like Toronto is so large as to be difficult to visualize.
I also note the remarks of the hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming). In addition to the items he mentioned, municipalities must buy equipment such as road machinery, fire trucks, and so on. Therefore, without question, adoption of the proposal would bring the municipalities great relief. I suggest that the point the hon. member raised is almost an argument for going the whole way. The government allows some exemptions now. I ask, why make the municipalities the bookkeepers and collectors of additional taxes levied with respect to pencils, paper and various other items municipalities use items which form a small proportion of the total value of the materials purchased? I know that the representatives of many municipalities feel as I do.
Some years ago there were 951 municipalities in Ontario. That number was reduced with the creation of new forms of government such as regional municipalities and the amalgamation of small municipalities. Today I believe there are in excess of 700 municipalities in Ontario. I feel that the federal government should say, in this particular case, "Why should we tax little brother, our municipal government, or our little grandson," as the case may be, "and extract the last pound of flesh. We do not want to tax in that manner. Therefore, the Department of National Revenue, excise division, will provide the municipalities with the necessary relief."
I say, why not be magnanimous, why not go the whole way and not collect such taxes from municipal governments? Our municipal governments are having a tough time raising money, most of which comes from real estate taxes. True, some people in the municipalities may have fair-sized homes, but their incomes are not necessarily in keeping with the size of their houses. If this motion were to pass and municipal councils could thereby save money, I am sure that they would channel these savings in the proper direction. For all these reasons, I hope the government will approve this motion.

If we are going to look at a new and revitalized constitution, we realize that we have to take care of the inequities, not only in the regions but also in the provinces and municipalities. It is time that the small municipalities and the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Reeves or the Canadian Federation of Mayors were involved in this dialogue. If we are going to look at a new and revitalized constitution to bring us up to date in the seventies, these people in the municipalities have to be involved. As the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) mentioned, they are the grass roots people, the ones who realize the problems of the local areas. An individual member has cognizance of the local problems, but sometimes we are a little too far removed from the people paying the taxes.
It has been proven in the past that when the government gets away from the people, it loses contact. If the constitutionalists get together, I am afraid they will not get the input from the people who will make this country work and make it run properly.
They have ideas at the municipal level. At one time I was a member of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Reeves and also of the small municipalities organization. I thought the talk at those conventions and the ideas that came from the small municipalities and the middle and larger municipalities has a more common sense base than we sometimes see federally or provincially. The mayors of those municipalities know the

problems of, taxation. They have been pushed in a corner over the past 50 or 60 years because of their lack of tax base.
As I mentioned previously, I certainly agree with this motion of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). We should support tax relief for the municipalities at all times because it is a double taxation. We are taxing them and they are taxing the people. We get money on one side from the federal tax and retax through the municipality. Because of their short and small tax base, they do not have the opportunity to have the taxing power they should possess. This could be done through constitutional change, but it is a two-way street. The provinces have to realize, maybe even more than the federal government, how much they have usurped the municipalities chance of taxation. This is for many reasons, maybe because bigger was better at some time in the past. Anyway they seemed to believe that. The municipalities know it is not true.
The municipalities are restricted so much in their taxing policy that their hands are tied. They are tied to the ordinary cost of increase on a current basis. Also, they are tied because of the major grants that come in. The municipalities have to come up with 20 per cent when somebody gives them 80 per cent. The tax dollar is a dollar that is spent federally, provincially, or municipally.
Another problem in the tax base is education. The municipalities are just a collecting agency for that. Indeed they are a collecting agency for which work they get no remuneration. If it were not going too far, I would say that maybe the school boards should collect their own taxes. However, I am afraid that would just add another bureaucracy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to enter this debate to make a very few comments. 1 want first to compliment the mover of the motion. It is a good motion, it has merit, and certainly should be debated in this House.
The municipality I come from certainly has some problems in raising the amount of revenue to answer all the demands that people living in the municipality place upon it, largely because it is a very fast growing municipality. At one time everyone thought that growth was a good economic thing. However, most municipalities are now finding that it is very costly.
I want to make a couple of comments on one or two points of which we should not lose track. First, there is a very fundamental point in terms of taxation. Whatever level of government is providing a service should be the level of government that is taxing for that service.
I would be very concerned if, over the years, the federal government became nothing more than a taxing organization and transferred most of the taxes it collected to the provinces which, presumably, in turn transferred a portion to the municipalities. That is a trend that has taken place over the past five or ten years. It has not been very healthy in our system of government whereby more and more or our federal tax revenues are transferred to the provinces and more of the provincial revenues are transferred to the municipalities.
I agree with the previous speaker in making the comment that as we enter into the national unity debate, particularly from a constitutional point of view, we should look at this point. In other words, we should redefine not only what might be the federal powers and those of the various provinces, but most definitely we should talk about what the powers of the municipalities should be as well. There are certainly responsibilities as seen by municipalities that might be as well or better handled by the provincial government, the same as there might be responsibilities carried out by the provincial government that should be vested with the federal government.
Most of the conversation we hear now about the Constitution deals with how much power the federal government should give to the various provinces. It should be on the record that there is a case to be analysed for three levels of government and to sort out clearly which ones have responsibility for which functions, and in turn look at the financing of them. That would be a much healthier situation than we seem to have at the present time where we are looking more and more at the federal government as a broad taxing organization, hoping that the taxation so raised is transferred to the provinces and passed in turn to the municipalities.
The whole question of accountability should surely be considered. If we go further in terms of exempting certain bodies from taxes, from increasing revenue passing from one level of
Excise Tax Act
government to the other, it seems to me it makes it almost impossible for the taxpayer to hold the various levels of government accountable for the taxation policies they have been following.
It seems to me another argument could be set out too, that is, whether an across-the-board exempting of federal sales tax is really effective in helping a municipality, or whether a municipality would be further ahead if it argued successfully for the federal government to take on as a share of the cost of some programs. Coming from a municipality which probably has one of the highest growth rates in Canada, I think one of the best things the federal government has done to aid that municipality for some time was under the federal housing action program whereby the government recognized the high cost faced by a municipality such as Brampton where such a large number of new homes are needed each year, and made available $1,000 per housing unit in accordance with criteria set out under the program. This seems to me to be a more useful approach than an across-the-board exemption from federal sales tax, because it speaks directly to a specific concern.
I also want to raise a concern which has been voiced by a number of municipal people about a program which, at the present time, is a very costly one to municipalities, that is, the arrangement for dealing with children who are in conflict with the law. Many times, when this situation arises, the court will determine whether these children should be looked after by the Children's Aid Society or whether they should be placed in private homes or homes run by private organizations. Of course the court makes the best determination it can, but a very different financial obligation depends on the decision. In one case the municipality gets a substantial amount of grant; in the other case the entire cost of the court decision falls upon the municipality. It seems to me we should be looking at some of these specifics and discussing how such a problem as that should be best handled by the sharing of the cost, rather than an across-the-board exemption of federal sales tax to municipalities.
When I was listening to my hon. friend from York West, I was impressed by the long list of articles municipalities can purchase free of tax. I was not aware that the tax exemption of municipalities was as wide as it is. But in spite of the long list read by the hon. member one could add a couple of more current exemptions which are very significant. One is the removal of federal sales tax from urban transit equipment. This was done to answer a very specific need, to promote urban transportation and to reduce the cost of municipalities. That is as it should be, because it is a national concern.
In the same category is the removal of federal sales tax from insulating materials. Energy conservation is the concern of every Canadian and this is a way by which the federal government wanted to assist in promoting energy conservation; it is doing this by means of a financial incentive which shows up.
I would rather see the federal government look at some of the specific programs which are difficult for municipalities to
5686

May 16, 1977
Excise Tax Act
handle, and perhaps participate in them, as opposed to giving across-the-board exemptions from federal sales tax at the municipal level. If tax exemptions are too wide you introduce the whole question of unfairness into the tax system in that some people are required to pay and others are not. One concern often expressed recently is that governments at all levels, including the municipalities, should be using private sector services a good deal more as opposed to employing people and building up a staff to handle all their problems in their entirety. If you were to exempt the municipalities across-the-board from federal sales tax it would go the opposite way to that argument.
In most cases it would be cheaper for the municipalities to do things themselves than to contract with the private sector which would be forced to pay purchase tax and which could therefore not compete on an equitable basis with the municipalities. I do not think that would sit very well with the private sector. They would have a very valid complaint if they were asked to be prepared to tender against the cost at which a municipality could carry out the service when the municipality was able to purchase whatever equipment or material it required free from sales tax. The hon. member might think about that aspect before pursuing the motion further.
I think all municipalities, in conjunction with the majority of provinces, and most certainly the federal government have worked very hard at keeping government expenses under control. Yet as I understand it, particularly in Ontario, the municipalities are obligated to budget for and collect school taxes without having any jurisdiction over what that level of taxation should be. I understand that the municipality I come from will this year issue separate tax notices to draw the attention of the people living in the municipality to which level of cost is which; people then can make their own judgment as to how prudent the municipality has been versus the education authority. I do not want to become involved in that debate except to raise the point that I think this is one of the concerns that municipalities have. It is the total tax bill that they have to present to the taxpayer that concerns them when they have some very legitimate programs that they want to proceed with and yet, of necessity, they must draw back because of increased education costs. I think this is the genesis of the pressure reflected in the motion. But the previous speaker made a good suggestion when he said that each level of jurisdiction providing services should be responsible for its own taxation. That is probably the better answer.
I just wanted to participate in the debate in order to raise two or three points which came to my mind as I was listening to the opening speeches this afternoon. I return to the point that we need to be very careful, in terms of our over-all taxation policy, to keep accountability within the jurisdiction which is providing the services. If you exempt municipalities and other bodies from federal sales tax, as has been suggested in a number of private members' bills and motions, you arrive at a situation where the federal government becomes a major taxing body whose programs consist mainly of transferring revenue to provinces. To my mind, this would not be in

keeping with federal taxation law. I appreciate having had the opportunity to add a few words to this debate.

May 16, 1977
Fisheries AFTER RECESS
The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. LeBlanc (Westmorland-Kent) that Bill C-38, to amend the Fisheries Act and to amend the Criminal Code in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND CRIMINAL CODE IN CONSEQUENCE THEREOF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I called it five o'clock I indicated it was my intention not to delay the bill but to make use of this opportunity to set forth a number of the concerns and worries of the fishermen on the west coast. Many of these stem from the recently concluded Canada-United States Reciprocal Fisheries Agreement which was signed, as 1 recall, just following the visit of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to Washington at the end of February. That document has not been referred to the committee so far. 1 am not even sure it has been tabled in the House. I feel it is one of the documents we should have available to us. I would ask the minister to make sure it is tabled in the House at the earliest opportunity because it is difficult to make specific reference to it without having the document in front of us, although there are a number of problems that have arisen out of it.
The purported purpose of the agreement was summarized in a document which reached me last week from the Pacific Trollers' Association. It is worth reading because it is pertinent to their present worries. The document reads as follows:
The bilateral agreement between Canada and U.S.A. sought to maintain fishery of both countries in accordance with existing patterns.
I see the minister nodding his head. This is what they were trying to do. It goes on to say:
Whilst both countries recognize that each has the right to manage fisheries within its jurisdiction within the terms of its domestic laws, the agreement nevertheless clearly spelled out that in the application of domestic laws, the contracting parties shall be guided by the principles of:
(a)	preserving existing pattern of reciprocal fisheries; and
(b)	in the case of reciprocal salmon fisheries, recognizing the interest of the state of origin in salmon spawned in its rivers.
This is a very good summary of the convention, as I understand it, but I do think it would be useful to have the text in front of us.
We are not sure whether the terms of this interim agreement have been fully implemented, because the ink on this agreement was barely dry when there was a recommendation
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
by the U.S. Pacific Regional Council which, to my understanding, undercut some of these principles. Here again I would like to cite this brief of the Pacific troller men because I think it sets forth their concerns as they see them. I am sure these are more than perceptions; these are facts which are facing fishermen today. The brief states that the fisheries plan of the United States Pacific Regional Council, which has now been promulgated into law, stipulates closures from April 15 to April 30, June 1 to June 30, and after September 15 north of Tillamookhead, and prior to the cohoe opening on July 1 mandatory use of single barbless hooks on all terminal gears. With the exception of the mandatory use of single barbless hooks such regulations which take 12 weeks out of the normal 26 weeks fishing in the area not even aimed at conservation.
What is worrying fishermen-and I am not sure this message is getting across to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc)-is that this denies one of the principles, if not both of those principles, underlined in the reciprocal agreement, that is, preserving the existing pattern of reciprocal fisheries.
Here is a unilateral action by one country, changing the terms under which fishing may be done in its waters. Granted, it is domestic law, but it is well known that Canadians Fish in U.S. waters just as U.S. fishermen fish in our waters.
Second, "They should recognize the interest of the state of origin in the salmon spawned in its rivers." This new recommendation by the U.S. Pacific Regional Council is likely to affect the salmon heading for the Fraser River. In other words, the United States unilaterally has made decisions about the fish heading up to the Fraser River. The use of gear, of course, is another unilateral decision.
As I indicated, the troller men in B.C. are worried about these moves, and having heard not only from troller men but also from others in the area, I feel there is a danger of retaliation by way of a request to close Canadian waters to U.S. fishermen. We have heard of the cod war in the waters of the North Atlantic. I do not think we want to see a salmon war on the Pacific coast, but unilateral actions of this kind, which belie and undercut an agreement which was concluded in good faith between both parties, could lead to some unfortunate actions.
On April 4 of this year I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) about an aide memoire, which I had been told was left with the State Department in Washington, concerning the application of certain domestic regulations to the fisheries on the west coast. As I understand it, that was a secret aide memoire. There was some misunderstanding. My question appears at page 4592 of Hansard. I asked that that aide memoire be tabled in the House. There has been no reaction from either the Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. However, there is a sneaking suspicion in everyone's mind that this aide memoire gave the U.S. authorities permission to go ahead with taking unilateral decisions affecting the fisheries off the Pacific coast. If that is not so-and I see the minister shaking his head in obvious disagreement-then I
May 16, 1977

suggest that the minister table this memorandum along with the reciprocal agreement so that we may all see them.
Of great concern to fishermen on the west coast are the consequences of the implementation of what is known as the Judge Boldt decision on Indian fishing. This gives U.S. Indian fishermen special rights, and as I understand the traditional principles underlying our reciprocal arrangements, the 50-50 split between Canadian fish caught by American fishermen and American fish caught by Canadian fishermen includes those fish which are taken by treaty Indians.
There has been a follow-up on this decison, and on my way back to Ottawa from my riding over the weekend I picked up the Sunday paper and there, large as life, was an account of where this might be leading. It is causing concern to a different group of fishermen because it seems that the United States granted the Indians the right to fish beyond the 12-mile limit with gill nets out in that area where they will have the first take of the fish coming into the Straits of Juan de Fuca. Whether this fear is real or imagined, it is there. It is causing fishermen concern, and I think this has to be examined very closely.
I mentioned the danger of a fish war off the coast. That is the kind of talk which appears in this article. I do not like to see it. I feel that the whole issue of the settlement of the division of the catch has to be dealt with immediately. The reciprocal agreement is fine provided it is lived up to, but it looks as though it is being undercut at every turn, and I therefore implore the minister to make sure that his officials are either inviting their counterparts from Washington to come here and talk these matters over, or going down to Washington to make sure that matters do not get out of hand.
First and foremost-and this is a principle which has been enunciated in this House-we must restore respect for treaty provisions. We do not want to undercut those provisions. We do not want to take unilateral action which would deny the undertaking we have given, and we certainly do not want those undertakings which have been given by another country to be undercut, to our detriment.
Still in this area of bilateral concerns on the west coast I come back to the extension of the boundary. I have been given to understand that there have been two or three submissions to the government in the last three or four weeks about the boundary line out to the 200-mile limit as promulgated in the Gazette. A new approach has been made, and I believe the province of British Columbia, among others, has suggested the San Juan trench as being the line which ought to define the boundary limits between the Canadian and the U.S. fisheries. This makes a fair amount of sense. I realize there is a problem regarding the trench on the east coast, but it is a principle that was accepted in New York, Geneva, and Caracas.
It has been accepted for a long time that if there are special circumstances that need to be taken into account in the definition or delimitation of areas, then those special circumstances could prevail over the median line approach. Here you
Fisheries
have an extension of the continental shelf out to the trench. It is a natural fishing area on the north side and on the south side where the fishermen of our two countries will know where they are. It is a navigational device as well and it will be readily known where that division lies. I am not arguing at all for the use of that approach on the eastern delimitation because I know that would deprive Canada of a great deal of her present resources.
When the parliamentary secretary makes his contribution to the debate, perhaps he will make some mention of the representations with respect to the Juan de Fuca trench. That is only part of the problem.
I am sure the minister is aware of the problems on the east coast, but I like to feel I am bringing some focus to the problems on the west coast as well. They are completely different, Mr. Speaker. It would not be out of place in the organization of the department to have an assistant deputy minister east coast and an assistant deputy minister west coast. The problems are distinct. Obviously the deputies would have to co-ordinate their activities, but I think this is something that should be considered.
Before the season opened there was a suggestion that a two-licence system be introduced on the west coast whereby a fisherman would have to choose this season whether he would fish inside the gulf or go out on the west coast of the island and fish there. It might even be narrowed down to the zone or the area. That would be followed a year later by a choice of gear. He would have to decide if he was going to be a seiner or a troller. The department decided he could not be both. This suggestion was thrown out to fishermen this year. It had been mentioned a couple of years ago, but the final decision to implement it was suddenly made public only weeks before the fishing season opened. This caused the fishermen, quite rightly, to ask for some other way of drawing up regulations.
In a brief presented to the British Columbia Progressive Conservative party caucus three or four weeks ago in Vancouver by the Fishing Vessel Owners Association of British Columbia, it was suggested that regulations by press release be eliminated. That sounds just like the House of Commons, Mr. Speaker. In this House we deplore the number of occasions when important statements that ought to be made here, where debate can follow, are made by press release or press conference. As we all know, the Prime Minister does not bother to speak in the House; he goes to another legislative chamber to make his statements. This is reflected again in the attitude of the government toward the manner of regulating whatever it is a minister is empowered to regulate. It is regulation by press release.
Fishermen seek an input in licensing and gear equality regulations, or some sort of consultative process which would enable them to express their views and get them across to demonstrate how reasonable are their views. The problems confronting fishermen today have been compounded by permitting licences on the west coast following an edict by the minister's predecessor that there be a reduction in the number of vessels. I do not think there has been a reduction, Mr. COMMONS DEBATES
May 16, 1977
Fisheries
Speaker. There seem to be more vessels fishing now than when the edict came down. What is happening is that the small fishing boats are being bought up and combined into big fishing boats in order to make them a viable proposition, so that instead of three, four or five-ton licences they get a 15-ton licence, and then they have to get a couple of sets of gear. They troll and they seine. This is causing trouble as it is over-capitalizing the industry. The minister has to sit down with the fishermen-not just with his officials on the west coast but with the fishermen-so that they can get their ideas across to him.
The business of area licensing was tossed around as something that was in prospect. Mr. Speaker, it is impractical in view of the nature of the quarry. Fishermen cannot see how they can be confined to a square area of the sea surface for fishing. Fish do no obey those regulations-they just go through them. They come up from the south and go through to the north, or go out sideways, and the fishermen must be free to pursue them, or face a bad season.
Then there is the problem of the sports fishermen. They are up in arms too. In this regulation by press release there was a suggestion that the sports fishermen were going to be licensed and that their catch was going to be reduced. The argument was that at present on the inside passage, where perhaps the major proportion of the sports fishing takes place, sportsmen are taking small fish and taking something in the order of five sevenths of the Chinook taken in that area. This five sevenths notion is being used to blow up the importance of the sports fisherman with respect to the whole Chinook fishery. I think this is an unfair approach to the whole operation. The commercial fishermen recognize this.
The chinook fishery is a large one and is not confined to the inside passage. With three, four, five and six-pounders being caught by sports fishermen, why is it not possible to suggest that a larger hook be used to catch a larger fish? They might not get so many, but a fisherman does not always go out just to catch fish; he goes out to enjoy himself, and if he gets fish that is a bonus. So the sports fishermen are up in arms on the west coast, as well as the commercial fishermen.
When our caucus was out on the west coast another area of sports fishing was brought to our attention, namely, the sports cannery trade. Sportsmen-if that is what they can be called-are flown in from the United States in large numbers, taken aboard a large yacht, then go out with their dorries or nets, catch fish in commercial quantities, cook them on board, put them in boxes, and then return to the United States with their fish already canned. That is not sportsmanlike. It is not sports fishing, and I am sure the minister agrees. There must be some way to control this operation. If sports fishermen had any sport in their blood whatever they would at least cast a line and troll, and then fight for what takes hold of the line. But this business of going in as a commercial venture and leaving with canned fish is a monstrous attack on our resources. I do not know if the minister can say how widespread this practice is; I gather it is of some sizeable proportions. It must be brought to an end.

Another problem besetting fishermen on the west coast is the special advantages available to Indian fishermen. They, I believe, pay only $10 for a licence, whereas a white man pays $2,000. I point out that boats of Indian owners are manned with white men. The Indians fish at a tremendous advantage, paying only $10 for a licence as against $2,000 their competitors must pay. True, native peoples have treaty rights, but surely the purpose of this assistance was to enable them to employ native peoples; it was not intended that they should employ white men hired from union halls.
One could raise other matters of concern. I have not mentioned the salmon enhancement program. I suspect we shall not push forward with the salmon enhancement program until there is a reciprocal agreement. Once such a reciprocal treaty is negotiated, we shall be assured of the benefit of fish spawned in our waters naturally or under the salmon enhancement program. I do not know the present state of this program but suppose it is almost inactive.
I will not deal with the matter of pollution. My colleague who has just resumed his seat I am sure will delve into these questions. Really, the only pollution matter I raise at this time, a matter on which I shall elaborate further on another occasion because I note that my time has almost expired, is the matter of the Kitimat tanker route. I am concerned about the damage which can be done in that area.
