speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND CRIMINAL CODE IN CONSEQUENCE THEREOF
speechtext: Thank you. I am concerned about the damage which can be done in the area if, God help us, it is decided to make Kitimat into a superport.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND CRIMINAL CODE IN CONSEQUENCE THEREOF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by applauding the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) for the excellent job he has done these past three years, and for introducing the amending bill before us. I think all hon. members will agree, whether they come from the east coast, Ontario, Quebec, or British Columbia, that the minister has treated all fishermen fairly. He has acted on behalf of fishermen, not on behalf of big fishing companies or moneyed interests. He has shown that he wishes to serve the small fishermen of Canada. For that I applaud the minister, and for introducing this bill and for his good work of the last few years.
I support this bill but give notice of my intention to raise one or two points during the committee stage. I hope hon. members will hasten the progress of the bill to committee, to allow regulations to be brought in as soon as possible. I understand that the B.C. Wildlife Federation have expressed their wish for this bill to be passed as soon as possible. They have indicated to me their full, 100 per cent support of these amendments.
I ask the minister to follow the precedent established last year by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) in allowing regulations to be submitted to members in committee. Let us see the regulations when the bill is in committee. We want to study the regulations at the same time as we study the bill.
May 16, 1977

Perhaps such a course would lead to speedy consideration and passage of this bill.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND CRIMINAL CODE IN CONSEQUENCE THEREOF
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND CRIMINAL CODE IN CONSEQUENCE THEREOF
speechtext:
As I recall, it was agreed to bring before the committee regulations pertaining to Bill C-83. This was done before the report stage. Unfortunately the session prorogued and the bill was never reported back. I think all committee members would consider it as a sign of the minister's trust and confidence if he were to let us see the regulations. That course, I suggest, would lead to orderly and speedy passage of the bill. The minister is present in the House, and I hope he has noted my supplication. I trust that I am not out of order, Mr. Speaker, in making these comments. To repeat, I commend the minister for bringing in this amending bill. As several members wish to speak, I shall not delay proceedings; however, I must raise one or two points of concern.
I applaud the provision giving fisheries officers the powers of peace officers. I understand fisheries officers will be given all the authority vested normally in peace officers, as set out in the Criminal Code. Such authority is to be used in certain ways. Since I represent a rural riding on Vancouver Island, I clearly understand that a fishery officer often has a difficult time dealing with poachers. If he catches one, he must summon an RCMP officer who issues the warrant, makes the arrest, and so on. Once this bill passes the fisheries officer will, for certain purposes, have all the powers of a peace officer, and for that I commend the minister. I foresee our fishery officers becoming useful instruments for the enforcing of our 200 mile limit.
Allowing fishery officers to act as peace officers in enforcing our fisheries regulations when they monitor the activities of distant water fishing fleets will lead to efficiency in manpower use. For example, consider what might happen if a fisheries officer were to board a Russian trawler operating off the west coast of Canada. He could monitor the size and type of catch and, if the licence issued by the minister has been contravened, he could in his capacity as peace officer issue the warrant, order the ship to enter harbour, or do whatever else is required in the circumstances.
Since he has the power vested in a peace officer, he need not send for the RCMP, or wait for the RCMP helicopter to put a member of that force on board ship. He has in his hands all the necessary power. I hope the minister will not take offence at my saying that there are not enough fisheries officers, at least in my part of the west coast, to do their job adequately.
I realize that the minister's department is under constraint and may not be able to hire enough staff, the work of which is measured in man-years of employment. His allocation of man-years is frozen, as is that of several other departments. But we must appoint more fisheries officers to monitor the area encompassing Thasis, Gold River, Campbell River, and all the other small communities of the region, which is several hundred square miles in area. Without adequate staff it will be impossible to monitor the area adequately and assume those additional responsibilities which fishery officers will have to
Fisheries
bear on the west coast and east coast of Canada. I trust fishery officers will be able to carry out the additional responsibilities with which they are to be entrusted. I add that they do an excellent job in Canada; they are dedicated, sincere people. I would only ask that their job be made a little easier by additional staffing, especially in the field.
Many times we staff our offices in Ottawa, Vancouver, or Saint John, but we do not staff the field, at least not as much as the bureaucracy. I say that with all respect. I feel that sometimes they are the forgotten men of the service. Anything we can do to aid them will be a plus, not only for the government, not only for the monitoring, but for their morale. They are very proud people. They do have a high morale, but we can help them out in that area.
One provision brought in by the minister in his amendment is ticketing for minor offences. This is a very rational move. Up until now, in many cases the fishery officers had to go into court on very petty offences. Our object should be to keep them in the field. They sometimes have to travel 50, 60 or 100 miles from their normal base of operation in order to appear in court, only to find that the person being prosecuted does not appear. That time is wasted.
We now have a provision whereby the fishery officers can issue tickets for minor offences, prescribed by regulations. I hope these regulations are given to us so that the committee members can judge what is a minor offence and what is not. In any event, through this regulation a voluntary plea of guilty can be entered and a prescribed fine sent in by the offender. There is no need for the fishery officer to leave his patrol area in order to appear in court on a very minor issue.
I mentioned in my earlier remarks the matter of poaching. This is a very serious matter which the bill will attempt to remedy. Off the coast of British Columbia, it is estimated that about 5,000 salmon are poached each year.
Salmon in British Columbia is approximately a $200 million industry. Poaching accounts for about $3.5 million. With the modifications in clause 58, I hope that a poacher can not only be fined or sent to jail, but that his equipment can be confiscated. That will add some teeth. Those people who take the salmon as they are going to the creeks and rivers to spawn are a menace to our salmon conservation and should be penalized to the utmost.
I mentioned to the minister in private conversation that those who act as the middleman between the poacher and the consumer should be equally flailed by the law, whether it be by confiscation of their trucks and equipment or by an increased fine. I understand there is a clause in the amendment which increases the fine from $1,000 to $5,000. Perhaps this can be clarified in committee.
The middleman makes the greatest profit, much greater than the poacher. These people should receive substantially increased fines, imprisonment, and confiscation of their equipment, the same as the poacher. I suppose it is analogous to the pusher of marijuana or other drugs and the person who

May 16, 1977
Fisheries
supplies the pusher. It is hard to distinguish which is doing the most damage.
Up until now we have had a maximum fine of $1,000 for the poacher. However, there are documented cases of the poacher being fined $500 even though he sold his catch for $1,000. This proves that in some instances crime does pay.
My biggest concern with regard to the poacher is not that he is illegally catching a fish, but destroying a resource which takes a long time to replenish. A great many of the 500,000 salmon that are caught are caught illegally on the way to the spawning grounds. This means there will not be young salmon returning the following spring.
If this continues year by year, with the salmon being illegally intercepted on their way to spawn, all the dreams of the Minister of Fisheries to enhance the number of salmon and to ensure that our children and grandchildren have the same pleasure and awe of nature in watching the salmon, will be for naught.
Because of greed, in order to make a dollar or $5, people are destroying a living resource unique in this world. The salmon has one of the most unique Canadian identities of any animal, bird or fish in Canada. Natives on the west coast regard it as a supernatural being because of the strength and endurance required by the salmon to reach its spawning ground; leaping over falls and travelling great distances. It is almost a miracle that the fish reaches the spawning ground. We want to ensure that the fish do spawn and that we have a return of the salmon each year.
The hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) mentioned some of the concerns of the west coast fishermen regarding some recent developments. I am not trying to deal only with the west coast, but that is the area I know best.
As the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich mentioned, there is concern about the two licence system. In reply to a question by the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. Pearsall), the minister stated there would be a one year moratorium. The two licence system will not be introduced in 1977. He went on to say that in addition to looking at the two licence system for the inside and outside fishery, he would look at the whole question of licensing. He will look at the dual fishing question, the combination boats, the gill netters and the patrollers, at the whole question of the conversion of one type of gear to another.
One of the great benefits the minister could bring the west coast fishery is something he announced in the maritimes a few months ago. He said he would set up a fishery advisory council. I hope there will be one for each coast, and perhaps one for the freshwater fishermen in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and so on.
On the west coast there are fishermen who are union members, sports fishermen, trollers, gill netters, seiners, and the Native Brotherhood of Fishermen. There is a great deal of gear and a lot of fishing. These fishermen, including the sport fishermen, would appreciate an advisory council so that they
[Mr. Anderson.)
could sit down with members of the minister's department in Vancouver, Nanaimo or wherever to discuss fisheries' policy.
Many fishermen feel the department makes decisions in isolation, and hands down decisions from on high. I realize that is an incorrect assessment. However, in order for the fishermen to feel part of the system there should be consultations every three or four months. The fishermen would feel much better if they knew what was taking place. They would feel they had at least a consultative role in the making of decisions, and I think the hon. gentleman's action would be warmly applauded.
As I began my remarks I stated that the minister was already well thought of by fishermen. My contribution is intended to make him even more popular. I believe the amendments he has brought forward are good for the fishermen and that they will be suported by all hon. members.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND CRIMINAL CODE IN CONSEQUENCE THEREOF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think Bill C-38 will find its proper forum in the standing committee and I, for one, am anxious to see that it gets there. I shall therefore be brief, though there are two things I want to say.
The amendments have been around for a long time, if my information is correct. I join with the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) in deploring the length of time it has taken to get thus far. I thought at one time the reason for the delay in first and second reading was that draft amendments were being considered by the various men and women in the provinces upon whom their enactment would have a profound effect. I thought that was the case, because when I was in British Columbia last August the field men who were responsible for the administration of this legislation had the draft amendments in their hands. In my view that was a good reason for the delay. I support that kind of consultation. I am in favour of the people in the field being given an opportunity to consider what the government has in mind. However, visiting the Atlantic provinces not long ago I was disappointed to find that the counterparts of the British Columbia field men had never heard of these amendments. This distressed me.
I do not have to champion the cause of British Columbia or of New Brunswick or of Newfoundland, but it would seem to me that if provincial public servants in British Columbia had the opportunity as long ago as August, 1976, and possibly even before that, to make some input into these amendments, surely their counterparts in all the other provinces concerned should have had an equal opportunity. Thus, when I find that this opportunity may not have been available in all the provinces- I say "may not" because it is possible that my information may be inaccurate-I am somewhat disturbed. Surely, of all pieces of legislation this is one which should be subject to the consultative process since, in many cases, it will be enforced by provincial public servants.
The minister has spoken of a meeting in the first week in June. 1 believe the official name of the group is the Council of Resource and Environment Ministers. The minister, in the
May 16, 1977

course of his opening speech, intimated he had received correspondence from some of his provincial counterparts expressing reservations about portions of this legislation. I understand that he has been urged to put off second reading until the council to which I have referred has had an opportunity to discuss the matter with him at that meeting in June. I do not think this is a terribly important consideration if the minister would agree that the provincial representatives on that council could appear before the committee so that the committee would have the benefit of hearing an expression of the reservations which the minister's provincial counterparts might have in mind.
I understand there are two general groups in the council. There are the representatives of provinces which make use of this legislation as their main anti-pollution law. Then there are others whose provinces have their own legislation, or which operate independently of the Fisheries Act. The real issue here is whether the legislation, either factually or perceptually, encroaches on the area of authority which the provinces have traditionally considered to be theirs in terms of the environment. This certainly appears to be the feeling of a number of the Atlantic provinces, and the same may be the case in British Columbia. This is the issue with which, I fear, we must come to grips.
A great deal of the authority in the areas of water and air pollution control which historically has belonged to the provinces is now, apparently, being assumed by the federal government through the medium of the Fisheries Act. There is no question in my mind that if one reads this bill and gives it a liberal interpretation, the provinces which are concerned about encroachment on their authority have real reason to be concerned. When, for example, one sees words like "water intake", "ditch", "channel" and so on, and when the bill starts talking about municipalities as polluters, or municipalities being creatures of the provinces, I can appreciate provincial concern in this area.
If there is one field in which I do not want to see confrontation between the federal government and the provinces it is that of the environment. It is the one area in which we must work in close concert if our efforts are to be successful, and that is why I hope the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry will, at an early meeting, deal with what I consider to be the key issue raised by this bill.
I echo what was said by the hon. member for Comox-Alber-ni (Mr. Anderson). The government has an unhappy record when it comes to legislating by regulation. I hope the committee will have an opportunity to consider the regulations, or at least their intent. I also hope we may hear from officials of the environmental protection service, if they give evidence, as to the manner in which they intend to enforce the regulations.
With respect to poachers, the minister said, virtually, that we had been licensing poachers; instead of preventing poaching, we have said to a potential poacher, "All right, if you want to go ahead and poach, this is what it will cost you if you get caught; it is a cost of doing business, the same as your boat, your flashlight, or whatever else you use."
Fisheries
There is no sense in the members of this House deploring what the. various courts have done when dealing with poachers. We all support the independence of the judiciary. That is surely part of our history of government. We also support the independence of the legislative arm. So if we are unhappy with what has happened with regard to poaching, let us not blame the judges; let us do something about it, but let us not wait from 1970 to 1977 to do something about it.
It was pointed out quite dramatically by my colleague from British Columbia, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, that when we had a $500 fine a poacher still made $500 profit because he had $1,000 worth of fish. But let us not blame the judges for that, let us blame ourselves. My colleague from Comox-Alberni says that he does not have enough inspectors in his riding but that he does not blame the minister. Well, I do blame the minister, and his predecessors, and the sins of his predecessors must be suffered by him. If I needed more inspectors in British Columbia, I know where I could get them; I would get them from all the planners in the Department of the Environment, these people whose raison d'etre is to say no. That is all they do, and the reason they say no is that if they said yes they would have no reason to exist.
When somebody in the field in the riding represented by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has a good project, he has a whole body of guys to whom man-hours are allocated here in Ottawa to say no. If the hon. member wants more inspectors in Comox-Alberni he should blame the minister for not providing them. He should tell him to move them out of planning. We have more planners than we have inspectors, so send them to Comox-Alberni, or wherever it is in the country that we have a shortage of these people.
I wish to make a few comments on the protection of the habitat, the amendments dealing with power to examine and approve plans of government and private sector development. In other words, in Bill C-38 the minister proposes to enter into a field which again I believe many provinces have considered traditionally their domain. Maybe my fears about that will be alleviated in committee. When I hear the minister say that we must have the power to examine and approve these plans, I am not too concerned about that aspect; what 1 am concerned about is that now we have another level of bureaucracy with which public and private developers must deal. I have no worry or concern about a potential development that does not or should not proceed on the basis of its potential damage to the environment. What I worry about is a development that should otherwise proceed but cannot in the face of another level of bureaucracy. This creates a frustration that simply does not permit that municipality or that private company to proceed with a development which otherwise would not be hazardous to the environment.
We all think developers are great, big, huge companies, or great, big, huge municipalities. Many are very small companies or very small municipalities. I say to the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, that at committee stage I will look for some assurance from the Department of Fisheries and the Environ-

May 16, 1977
Fisheries
ment that their concern about protecting the environment is not going to be manifested in the creation of a bureaucracy that would impede otherwise acceptable developments. Small businessmen and small municipalities tell me that their main frustration is having to deal with too many levels of government and, within each level, with too many inspectors, too many forms, too many administrative tribunals. Therefore, when this bill comes to committee-and I hope it will come very soon-I think we should examine that aspect with great care.
With respect to water pollution the minister is, I believe, moving-and likely rightly, although I think we should talk about this to some extent in committee-to the "polluter pay" principle. I think that is what he said in his remarks earlier this afternoon. That is likely a good principle. 1 am concerned with the identification of the polluter. If he is identifiable, then likely the principle that he should pay is a good one. The minister has said, though, that inspectors designated by the department will have more power, and again I worry about those provinces that appoint their inspectors and those that do not. Again we have a division here, two types of provinces dealing differently with this particular part of the Fisheries Act.
With regard to offshore pollution, I think the minister said that 80 per cent of such pollution comes from land. I am not terribly impressed by figures. I ask, 80 per cent of what kind of pollution? How is it measured, and in what areas? If the major source of pollution in Kitimat, for example, comes not from the hazard of moving tankers through an apparently treacherous passage, fine, I agree with the minister we should be more concerned with pollution coming from the landward side. But 1 do not know on what he bases his figure of 80 per cent; I hope that we get into that in committee.
One thing in the minister's remarks which concerned me was his reference to our ineffectiveness to act against polluters as compared to that of the United States. He referred to a special agency. I presume he is referring to the environmental protection agency. I ask the minister to remember that we are comparing apples and oranges. That is an independent agency. If the minister is about to move the environmental protection service out of his department and create an agency out of it, that is a different thing. I think it is not very helpful to compare the U.S. situation with our own when we are dealing in the U.S. with an independent agency and in Canada with a service in the department. I simply point that out gratuitously, Mr. Speaker, to the minister, because I do not think the comparison is particularly helpful in terms of this debate.
In summary, I look forward to this legislation moving into committee, though I am not anxious that it move with haste through committee. We sat around for a good number of years waiting for these amendments. I have a great respect for the integrity of my colleagues who serve on that committee. I think their determination is to have good, viable, enforceable legislation. Therefore I hope the minister looks forward to examination of this bill in some length and in some detail, with the benefit of the expertise of witnesses, particularly those who
[Mr. Jarvis.l
will help us in regard to this federal-provincial conflict which I think is very real.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND CRIMINAL CODE IN CONSEQUENCE THEREOF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before making a few remarks on Bill C-38, I think all hon. members will join me first in extending congratulations to the minister who holds this important portfolio; he is noted for his qualifications, his tenaciousness and his determination to try and help this class of citizens, rich or poor, persevere in the practice of one of the oldest trades in the world; we now call them professional fishermen.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, fishing is regarded as an essential activity which is of prime importance for many reasons. You have only to think that more than 55,000 Canadians depend essentially on fishing for their living and 22,000 are in the fish processing and marketing industries. Furthermore, I think that the annual return of the fishing industry in the economy is over $1 billion; it should be added that exports account for half this figure.
In the Atlantic provinces as in other areas in eastern Quebec, three quarters of the towns and rural areas depend on fishing to a certain extent. It goes without saying that outside of social welfare, allowance, old age security and the like, agriculture and logging, that is the only source of livelihood for the many Canadians and fishermen living in those areas.
Mr. Speaker, I must add that on the west coast fisheries are also very useful but it must be said that the fishing industry there is of relatively little importance to the prosperous economy of British Columbia. On the other hand, on the east coast, of which I am one of the representatives, the situation is different in that fishing, whether we like it or not, is of almost incalculable importance. In fact, that is the part of Canada where the federal government must increase supervision, particularly off the shore of Halifax and St. John's, in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and in the North Atlantic, rather than in western coastal waters. One can readily claim, Mr. Speaker, that fishing is not only a way of life or one occupation among others for coastal communities in Canada, but that it is, to my mind, the only means of livelihood, if not the only possible way of life for most of them. In Canada, let us recognize it, our fishing resources are being threatened and it is now more than high time our governments attend to rebuilding our fishing stocks; otherwise, we will find ourselves at some point in time without those invaluable resources.
A quick look at Bill C-38 reveals, Mr. Speaker, that it stipulates that in the future, persons may be designated as fishery officers, as meant by the act, and even classes of persons deemed qualified to act in that capacity.
Those last amendments to the Criminal Code and the one proposed in clause 20 will in effect give fishery officers the powers of peace officers.
Although in general agreement with Bill C-38's provisions, I would like to call the minister's attention to certain discrepancies. It is very well to refer to environment and conservation, but an advertisement campaign would be needed to inform the
May 16, 1977

public at large, from grade school to all spheres of society. It should promote conservation, and above all the love and respect for nature and everything that contributes to the beauty of one's area, province and country.
The time is over when the sea's biological resources were considered inexhaustible. In 1968, 42 per cent of the world's fish stock was caught and for the first time in 1969, there was a reduction in year-to-year world landings. There is no doubt in my view that conservation prompted the government to introduce such a bill, because it is a fact that fishery products, as any other goods, are subject to the law of diminishing returns. For that reason calls have been heard in past years against free deep sea 'fishing, which had been the rule heretofore.
Considering the current situation of Fishery resources, clearly absolute freedom in deep waters is no longer in order, especially since new production techniques have brought a revolution in various traditional forms. We need only remember that the sailor-fisherman used to be the main factor of production. Nowadays, highly sophisticated fishing ships, gear and techniques have come to the fore. It is therefore urgent that the government take regulatory measures to prevent the serious economic dangers now facing us.
Mr. Speaker, Canada has the second longest seacoast in the world. It can even be called the longest, if we also consider the Arctic of course. Moreover, the continental shelf of our country is quite large and includes important resources. It is the second largest in the world and makes up a surface equal to 40 per cent of the territory.
Off the west coast, the continental shelf is rather narrow, I agree, but in the eastern area it extends as far as 400 miles in the Grand Banks area. Its coastal waters contain important fishery reserves, particularly in the Grand Banks to the east of Newfoundland. The latter is no doubt highly essential for the coastal provinces of Canada, both socially and economically. Those are, Mr. Speaker, a few reasons why the federal government should keep on introducing measures to have an ever increasing control over our coastal waters.
It is more and more urgent that the government take serious measures to preserve the stocks and prevent Canadian fishermen from being endangered by those who traditionally fish not far from the Canadian coast and have huge fleets and vessels which, for all practical purposes, take the daily bread away from Canadian fishermen along the east and the west coasts of our country.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that Bill C-38 will meet our wishes and that all those who earn a living from that noble occupation will not have to face disappointment and at last will see better days.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND CRIMINAL CODE IN CONSEQUENCE THEREOF
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to say a few words on the bill. I will keep my remarks brief because there are
Fisheries
other people on both sides of this House who want to make comments. It is important to tell the minister, on behalf of the east coast, that we appreciate the measures brought forward in this bill. I want to echo the words of my colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson), who generally congratulated the minister on the job he is doing in his portfolio. Certainly the people in the east, and particularly in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, are cognizant of the policy measures he has brought forward while he has been the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. That has not gone unnoticed in the province, and we appreciate what the minister is doing in the field of fisheries because more and more the Newfoundland economy must depend on that particular resource.
I am glad to see my member of parliament entering the Chamber because I want to make him aware of the problems on the east coast. These measures to toughen up pollution laws are very important. The fishery in Newfoundland is the backbone of the economy there and will remain so. If we are to protect that renewable resource, then certainly we must bring in measures which are tough enough to deal with the nonrenewable resources as they are transported over that marine habitat. I think it is a good idea to broaden the terms of the bill to include the habitat as well as the fish. Also, the tougher measures on clean-up are certainly a welcome addition to the legislation as it exists at the present time. However, I want to draw attention to two other aspects of the bill which I think are important. One is the amendment with regard to trawler fishing.
There is an inherent conflict between the offshore fishery and the inshore fishery, and keeping seiners and trawlers outside a certain limit gives inshore fishermen breathing space to harvest their share of the resource.
From time to time the minister has given firm commitments to the inshore fishery. This amendment shows that he certainly meant what he said, and I welcome that. There are trawlers which are now interrupting the fishing of inshore fishermen in my area and, I am sure, all over the province and, indeed, throughout eastern Canada. This amendment will certainly help them and will cut down on the conflict between offshore and inshore fishermen.
Another point I want to draw attention to-and my colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni also referred to it-is the amendment which would give fisheries officers the authority of peace officers as set out in the Criminal Code of Canada. Last spring the sealing operation was a topic which did not go unnoticed in the House of Commons or across this country. Unfortunately, much misinformation has been disseminated with regard to that industry, and it is going to be difficult to turn the tide. I think that those journalists who went to St. Anthony this year, who looked, and who bothered to find out the facts, wrote the truth, and I think the tide is now turning in favour of the sealing industry in the province. Newfoundlanders want to earn a living. They must have the

May 16, 1977
Fisheries
income which comes from that particular lucrative hunt to supplement their yearly incomes, and it is entirely necessary that it be kept going. The methods used are the most humane that can be devised.
It is a myth that the seal is in danger of extinction. The quota is well within limits. There is a harvestable quota every year, and certainly there will be one next year as well. Phony conservationists such as Mr. Davies, and other organizations which took part in protesting the seal hunt, are starting to be known for what they are. Bona fide conservationists in this country, people in legitimate humane societies, are showing them up for what they are because these phonies call into question the whole of the humane movement in this country.
On the ice this year a number of people interfered with the seal hunt, and it was impossible to enforce the Criminal Code even though seal pelts were taken from sealers and thrown into the water, and even though clubs were taken and thrown away. In other words, these people were interfering with sealers in the course of carrying out their work, and it was impossible to lay any charges against them. RCMP officers were eventually on the ice, but not when they were really needed, and this amendment to make fisheries officers peace officers will be a step in the right direction in dealing with people who insist on interrupting bona fide fishermen in the course of their work. That certainly is a welcome amendment to my part of the country.
I want to make my own contribution to the Fisheries Act, in conjunction with the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). The hon. member spoke in this debate this afternoon. He referred to the amendment which we will be moving jointly. A petition which we have drawn up is now being circulated in the province of Newfoundland and Labrador, and already we have thousands of signatures to that petition. I want to put on the record what the petition says, and repeat that when this bill comes before the committee we intend to move a further amendment to the Fisheries Act to incorporate the principle of that petition in that act. The petition is as follows:
THAT greater protection be given through law to sealers by amending the Fisheries Act and regulations.
THAT all ways and means of tightening the Fisheries Act and sealing regulations to give adequate support and protection to sealers be explored.
WHEREFOR it would be an offence for any person in any vehicle or aircraft or boat to come within a defined sealing area without a permit from the Minister of Fisheries, and further that it would be an offence to take or destroy property or otherwise to interfere with a sealer or sealing ship in the course of their working during the sealing season.
That petition is going to be presented to this House very shortly. The hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe, other members of parliament from Newfoundland, and I, have distributed this petition, and we are hoping for thousands of names so that we can let this House know exactly how important this issue is in our province. Thereafter we intend to move an amendment to the Fisheries Act so that next year proper protection can be given to those people in the legitimate pursuit of their livelihood, and so that we can take appropriate action against those phony conservationists who destroy the

reputation of hard working people in a cause which is entirely questionable.
I want to conclude my remarks by congratulating once again the minister for bringing forward these amendments, and to say to him that his efforts have not gone unnoticed by the people on the east coast. They are very grateful for the policy he has brought forward, beginning with the 200-mile limit. Of course there have been other measures which the minister has brought before the House as well.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage it is very difficult to be anything but repetitive. I regret very much that I find myself in this position. However, there are some characteristics of the comments which have been made which leave room for expansion and for emphasis to be placed upon the distribution of problems throughout Canada as they have existed in the fishing industry.
I am very disappointed that there has not been an adequate force of people available as enforcement officers for the Fishing regulations as they apply to salmon in the fresh waters of New Brunswick. I am sure the minister is aware of the problem which exists. It has been mentioned many times in this House. It has been mentioned by the press of New Brunswick, and it has been very clearly emphasized that it is indeed a cynical and unlawful group which persistently, habitually, and for economic gain poach salmon in the streams of New Brunswick. They have challenged the law enforcement body of the department. They have mocked that body. They have made it impossible for law enforcement to exist.
It was mentioned today that there was a 50 mile portion of stream for one man to look after in Newfoundland. The hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe mentioned this. There are many remote streams in many parts of the Atlantic area which are rarely if ever seen as far as supervision of the salmon population is concerned.
In my memory this particular stream abounded with fish. The climax has been long in coming, but evident as it approached. At one time in the Saint John River and the Miramichi River permits were given for nets. They were an integral part of the land grant along those streams, part of the livelihood, the food supply of those who first settled there. The nets were allowed to be put in place on an unlimited basis initially, a regulated basis at a later date, and were removed totally some years ago. Now they are only allowed to net salmon in the Bay of Fundy. The population in the Saint John River has been declining for a long time; it did not receive adequate attention at an early enough date.
I am sure the minister is aware that poaching in the Toiboque River became such a problem that last season the river had to be closed. This was a serious detriment to those people who depended on sports fishing for their livelihood. It is a challenge to the enforcement capability of government. It was found wanting. When the government admits its incapa-
May 16, 1977

bility by closing the stream because it cannot control it, that is indicative of laxity in the administration of existing legislation.
I hope this new legislation will give more strength to the enforcement group and that the minister will find some means to bring things under control. In the control of human society we have found reasons to take extra measures in case of emergency. We find ourselves with respect to the salmon streams of the Atlantic provinces and apparently also in the ocean on the west coast, in a position of emergency. Whatever measures should be taken must be taken. Wherever manpower can be found it must be utilized to put lawless people out of business. They rank with the rustlers of the past.
The salmon enhancement program for the Atlantic area needs additional attention, as was mentioned by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). We have not followed the example of other jurisdictions. We impeded the progress of salmon upstream when there were hydro developments in the Atlantic area. When this was done in Scandinavia, spawning grounds were developed, and stream mouths were filled with gravel or whatever was necessary to create the spawning area that had been taken away by virtue of the construction of a dam on the stream. We have not done this. We have actually reduced the number of young salmon being hatched in our federal hatcheries.
There was a time when the hatchery next door to my home produced over a million salmon a year. The count is seriously down relative to the efforts made in the 1920's-not the 1940's, 1950's or 1960's but in the 1920's-to enlarge the salmon population of our streams. We have cut back in this regard. One hatchery has been closed, and the capacity of others has been reduced. The money voted for hatchery operations has been reduced to the point that supervisors are wondering how they will be able to operate their premises even with the reduced number of fish assigned to them. This is indicative of knowing about a problem but not putting any real effort into correcting it.
I want to thank the minister for the position he has taken in respect of the proposed Eastport refinery and the hazards to the environment had an oil refinery been built there. I hope the measures he is prepared to take will prohibit any such construction.
Earlier in the session I mentioned that a modern, up-to-date, and accurate chart of the waters of Head Harbour Passage and the adjoining areas through which the oil tankers would have to pass, is not available. I am happy to learn that a survey is now in progress which will chart those waters and give the department a strong case to present to anybody who might be concerned about construction of the refinery.
One of the problems that has arisen from the restrictive licensing which the department has introduced is that communities on the Atlantic coast find themselves with only one source of livelihood by virtue of their geography, namely, fishing. Licensing has been restrictive, quotas imposed, and the seasons shortened, and these people have found themselves with a declining standard of living.
Fisheries
It had been traditional in the fishing areas of Canada, as it had been in the agricultural areas, that the family of a fisherman might wish to fish, as the family of the farmer in the past had wished to farm. There is no longer any possibility that this can take place. Within the last few weeks I wrote to the minister about the plight of one of these people, asking that he be granted the licence he had requested. By virtue of a change in the boats in the area, particularly the seiners, by the addition of refrigeration, the carriers who used to service the seiners to carry their fish to market were out of a job. A 70-foot boat is a major investment. This man who had one now has nothing for it to do. A lifetime investment is tied up to the dock, and there it will remain.
This is the kind of regulation of the fishing industry about which previous members have spoken. Those working at a desk adjoining a marble corridor in Ottawa have no conception of the social impact of the denial of permission to make a living in the traditional way in which that family has lived for generations. Who in this House would sit quietly while a 70-foot boat rotted out the rest of its life tied up to a pier, because of regulations imposed upon the fishing community? There is a social responsibility on the department to conserve the stocks, but there is also a social responsibility to do it in a way whereby people who have had the habit of fishing those stocks, do not starve.
A number of fishermen along the coast of the Atlantic area have been denied more than one licence, yet for generations they might have fished lobsters in the fall, and fished handline in the summer. They might have worked in three or four of the fisheries in the area. Today, if by any chance they have failed to renew a licence for the fishery in which they had by habit participated, they find they can no longer re-establish themselves. This has created hardship. If they miss the deadline for the renewal of the licence they held-they find they no longer have a licence.
Social consideration is essential. This applies to pollution as well. Many hard remarks have been made about those who have polluted freshwater and salt water, but what some people have failed to recognize is that all the laws of the land perhaps have been adhered to, and it is only as a result of changing laws that we now call pollution, "pollution". It is only with expanding industry that the capability of a particular stream is over-stressed by added pollution.
I was rather impressed by an environmentalist in British Columbia who was a senior member of the department of the environment there. He said dogmatically that, although we are concerned about the environment, we must recognize nature can absorb a certain amount of pollution, and that if pollution is below critical levels, no measurable damage will be done to the environment, or to human beings or animals living in it. He said his department was monitoring the level of certain additives found in the waters of British Columbia. If those additives were within certain limits, the department of the environment in B.C. was not particularly worried. They worried when the level of pollution exceeded the tolerance of the environment, that is to say, the ability of any part of the environment,

May 16, 1977
Fisheries
whether air or water, to absorb the pollution without measurably harmful effects.
We have not recognized the social responsibility shown by some who discharge pollutants into the environment. As the minister mentioned, some industries have traditionally operated at a particular location. The pollution resulting from such operations was within the tolerance limits suggested by that B.C. official as acceptable. The level of pollution was tolerable, until that pollution was supplemented with other pollution coming from some other point within that ecosystem.
Many polluters, be they small communities on river banks or small industrial concerns, have not the financial strength to finance the acquisition of anti-pollution equipment. Therefore the correction of this situation becomes a social responsibility. The more quickly the government recognizes that it must provide money to those who lack the means to install anti-pollution equipment, the more effective its environmental efforts and anti-pollution programs will be. What is more, they will be more acceptable to the general public, for if the government puts its money where its mouth is, so to speak, society will look with a keener eye at the requirements of the department.
As the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis) said, the bill we are discussing has, so to speak, ruffled a few feathers in the provincial structure of this country; for that reason it is not timely. We have heard across this nation provincial governments complaining of the federal government's intrusion into their domain. This bill adds to that intrusion. We have in this country a vast duplication of services.
Perhaps, by way of example, I could mention something the mayor of Toronto said some time ago. Discussing a certain program with members of this House, the mayor mentioned a certain federal government program relating to the conduct of the city of Toronto. He said that there were moneys available to the city of Toronto under federal programs. He went on to say that the city of Toronto and its sister municipalities had negotiated with the federal government for several years with respect to the policy about which he was talking, but at the conclusion of seven years no agreement had been finalized in the field of housing.
In this country we find ourselves beset with municipal, provincial, and federal regulations, and it is almost impossible to cut through this maze of red tape. One finds that when one has cleared the hurdle of one department, one must deal with another department which says, "No, you cannot do this." There is no longer a single voice in the federal government which can answer our environmental concerns. The answering voice may be that of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) or of the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), or it may be that of the Department of Fisheries. Each may present a separate view and take a different direction. It is awfully difficult to correlate all these views. I wish all these people would sit down at a table and resolve this difficulty.

This bill is an intrusion into provincial rights. I join with the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot in saying, for goodness sake, let us bring all these people together around a table and simplify these procedures as best we can. Let us not intrude further on provincial rights concerning pollution controls. Such intrusion is becoming a habit with the department. Before the present minister was appointed to his portfolio, the provisions of the act which related to pollution in off-shore waters under the jurisdiction of Canadian pollution regulations overlapped the provisions of that act which controlled the environment of the shore. That act, in turn, overlapped the provisions of another act which controlled our land environment. All three acts overlapped, to some extent. Each act was administered separately. Mr. Speaker, we do not want this sort of thing. Let us bring all this pollution legislation under one package. Let us put the provinces in the position of being able to administer. This three or four tier interference with development is not what this country should have to endure.
I come now to the regulations which will be promulgated under this legislation. First, let me speak of a regulation of which I am sure the minister is unaware and the reason for which nobody has bothered to explain, which created great hardship. Those familiar with the fishery know that a fisherman is allowed to cure his own fish. He may put the fish in salt, or in brine, or smoke it, and so on; or, he must sell the fish to somebody else who will market it, cure it, or otherwise deal with it. Mr. Speaker, the minister has been most attentive today; perhaps he will pay close attention to what I am about to say.
Does the minister know that if I were a fisherman and filled my boat in one day with fish, I would not be permitted to hire help for cleaning and scaling that fish for treatment? I am not allowed, Sir, to hire help for cleaning and scaling that fish. Did the minister know this? Speaking of regulations, I wonder if the minister is aware of another regulation to which I shall now allude.
Not long ago an inspector of his department entered a processing plant of smallish size which was processing salt fish. The height of the ceiling over the tanks in which the fish were held was less than eight feet. The plant owner or manager was advised that he could clean his tanks but could not load them again until the height of the ceiling had been raised at least to eight feet. I made inquiries. The bacteria count was not the trouble; there was nothing about the fish to make it hazardous for human consumption. Apparently the inspector was about six foot six tall and had bumped his head on the ceiling. I can see no other explanation for his wanting the ceiling higher off the ground. Certainly ceiling height over the tanks had little to do with fish being soaked in brine. Apparently the inspector had invoked some regulatory authority. I cite this example, because this bill will provide officials with even greater regulatory powers.
Quite possibly the minister might not be aware of all the regulations. I suggest, in the case of this bill, that perhaps a codicil should be added. Any regulations made under this bill should be placed before the fisheries committee of the House
May 16, 1977

of Commons for consideration and discussion before they descend with any hardship upon those who would be regulated. This would gain some publicity. I can assure hon. members that the little guy on the coast does not read the Canada Gazette which makes this official. He is only made aware of this by somebody dropping in to tell him that he is breaking regulation ZYX which was passed the day before yesterday, and something should be done about it.
All those who have spoken have made an important contribution. I am sure those who are interested in the fishing industry along the Atlantic and Pacific coasts will read with considerable interest the remarks of the minister, of the hon. member for South Shore, and of members from British Columbia and Newfoundland. I hope the minister will not only take careful note of those remarks but will go one step further.
The minister's predecessor created a precedent by permitting groups to come before him and the fisheries committee to present their problems and make recommendations. Those committee meetings at which organizations from British Columbia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland appeared were some of the most interesting and informative meetings that have been held under the jurisdiction of the minister in the five years it has been my privilege to be here.
Those meetings should become habit. It would benefit the direction of research, the minister, and the fishermen. It would create a better feeling between the fisherman and the minister and his officials. It would be a good will gesture to make this an annual event.
Various agricultural organizations appear before the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and his departmental officials on a regular basis, sometimes more than once a year. Why not the various fishing associations? I do not mean the industrialists who process, but the people from the shore. Why not permit them to appear before the minister so that he can understand the problems as they arise for them from day to day and year to year? We know they cannot all be resolved at once.
I hope the minister will do these two things: first, before applying the regulations place them before the committee and, second, on an annual basis have liaison with the people in the boats by allowing their delegations to appear before him and a committee of the House of Commons to consider the problems as they arise.

I have just returned from Williams Lake, British Columbia, in the heart of my constituency, where the British Columbia Wildlife Association held its 1977 convention. One of the key matters being discussed was Bill C-38. After three hectic days, they learned of the possibility of this bill being brought before the House. I assured them that my colleagues on both sides of
Fisheries
the House would get this most important bill through the House and into committee.
I welcome the few minutes available to me to make that point. I wish to point out in particular that the British Columbia Wildlife Association were most emphatic that all British Columbia members should realize that this bill must get into committee as soon as possible. I sincerely hope it will be put to a vote this evening.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-POSSIBILITY OF INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY TO AVOID FUTURE HIGH LEVELS OF UNEMPLOYMENT
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-POSSIBILITY OF INDUSTRIAL STRATEGY TO AVOID FUTURE HIGH LEVELS OF UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate tonight arises out of the unsatisfactory answer given to a question put by myself to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on March 16 as it appears in Hansard at page 4029. On that day I asked the Prime Minister the following:
As we now, unfortunately, live with an unemployment figure of one million, would the Prime Minister tell us whether any steps have been taken at least to evolve an industrial strategy for Canada to ensure that in the coming years this chronic type of unemployment will not continue?
The Prime Minister startled the House by replying:
The House has heard on different occasions statements on elements of our industrial strategy by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I think one of the reasons the country is in difficulty is that Canadians are living beyond their means.
I would point out that this is a typical response of the Prime Minister and that it demonstrates the total lack of understanding he has concerning the economic morass into which the country has slumped.
If we are to look at the single, most important reason why we have regional divisions in the country, yes, even the belief in certain areas of the country that separatism would be better than remaining within Confederation, we should look first and foremost to the economic condition that the government has
May 16, 1977

allowed the country to get into. This was borne out, I point out, by the Toronto Star survey which appeared last Saturday which outlined the fact that in Quebec, for example, the number one concern is not what the Prime Minister has misrepresented it to be. The number one concern in Quebec is the economic condition of that country and the fact that people are going without jobs in that country. I say that is due to the lack of an industrial strategy on the part of this government.
That is the essence of the question. If we accept the fact that we do have an unsatisfactory economic situation in Canada today, then what is the government going to do in the next few years to develop an industrial strategy which will ensure that we will get out of the present morass? There is nothing new about this question, Mr. Speaker. For example, in September, 1970, the Economic Council of Canada, in a booklet entitled "Performance and Potential", dealing with the period from mid-1950 to mid-1970, outlined to the government, chapter by chapter, what it should do to ensure that our economy would not slip as it has. At page 76 of the report the following statement appears:
We feel strongly that there should be an accelerated movement towards the evolving practice of planning further ahead-say, over five-year periods-by governments, business and other groups, and jointly with other countries in international organizations.
At page 79 of the report it is stated:
It is becoming almost trite to suggest that there continues to be a requirement in Canada for greater co-ordination of policies-within governments, between governments, and between the public and private sectors.
I am simply saying that it is the government's failure to adopt this economic course which has led to the feeling of disintegration which exists in this country. In short, many people in the country are saying, "We have had enough; we want out". I think it is time the government countenanced that it has the heaviest responsibility of any body in this country for the state we are in.
Dealing again with the report of the Economic Council of Canada, at page 84 the council states:
A major concern of this report is that the Canadian economy has fallen significantly below its potential. A quick return to potential is not feasible. But the central challenge is to begin to close the gap between actual and potential performance as soon as possible-to begin to reduce the significant human and economic costs of high unemployment-bearing in mind the need to maintain reasonable stability of prices. It is important to recognize that the present degree of slack, reflected partly in high unemployment, will tend to persist and grow until an annual rate of real growth in excess of 5 per cent is resumed.
Unfortunately conditions have deteriorated since 1970. Here are the facts, Mr. Speaker. Since 1970 we have had 65 per cent inflation. Unemployment has jumped from below 5 per cent to the present 8.3 per cent, with one million people out of work. In 1970 we had a budgetary surplus of $392 million. This year it is projected that we will have a budgetary deficit-I emphasize deficit-of $7.2 billion. Even that deficit of $7.2 billion was not understood by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) until he went to a committee of this House and was told by his officials that in truth he had in his budget speech outlined a $7.2 billion deficit.
Adjournment Debate
Our current account trade deficit has gone from a surplus in 1970 of $1.1 billion to a deficit of $4.9 billion in each of the last two years, and of course, as we know, real growth in the country has continued to slump. That is why I once again put to the Prime Minister the question: what is the Prime Minister going to offer this country in the form of an indusrial strategy to ensure that, at least by the mid-1980's, we are not in a still worse position than we are in today?
As we all know, we have been borrowing heavily, both externally and in the domestic market, to cover deficits run up by governments in Canada. When I asked the Minister of Finance on May 3 in the committee when he saw us getting a balanced budget, he replied: "I don't know that I could project an early date for that".
Then he added:
... I do not anticipate it will be easy to get that deficit down very quickly.
In short, if there were a proper industrial strategy and if there were proper direction from the federal government, I can assure you we could return to a sounder economic base, with relatively low unemployment and relatively low inflation. Nothing would ensure the continuation of Confederation and the death of separatism in this country more quickly than to give people the real growth they are entitled to.

subtopic: CONFEDERATION-POSSIBILITY OF ESTABLISHING THIRD ORGANIZATION CONCERNED WITH UNITY

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: CONFEDERATION-POSSIBILITY OF ESTABLISHING THIRD ORGANIZATION CONCERNED WITH UNITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for interrupting the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Poulin). I want to address myself to a response I received from the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen), the Acting Prime Minister, last Friday, with respect to the establishment of a third bureaucracy in regard to the whole issue of national unity.
The remarks of my distinguished colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), are very appropriate about some of the underlying causes of the feeling of separation in the province of Quebec. The gross failure of the government to deal with some of the fundamental economic issues in this country, and particularly in the area of Quebec,

have been brought to our attention very, very vividly by the latest Toronto Star poll. Notwithstanding the rhetoric we hear from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and others in the government, the fact of the matter is that the underlying feeling in the province of Quebec is that they are not receiving a fair and reasonable deal under this particular government.
Considerable speculation has arisen from statements made by the Prime Minister himself in his press conference with respect to the role and function of Mr. Jean-Luc Pepin in a national unity commission. The Prime Minister referred to the possibility of Mr. Pepin fulfilling a function in some new type of national unity commission. It is to be a high profile commission. The Acting Prime Minister was unaware of any possible appointment, so I assumed from that there is absolutely no danger that there will be any further bureaucracy brought into play with respect to this particular commission. If that is the case, and if the parliamentary secretary can confirm that there is not another commission being contemplated by the government, then in a sense that is a very welcome announcement, because the Prime Minister has been creating new bureaucracies with respect to the question of national unity at breakneck speed.
I suggest that bureaucracies are substitutes for constructive proposals. An attempt is being made to submerge the whole debate into a number of agencies and sub-agencies studying the effects and consequences of separation of the province of Quebec from Canada. I suggest that this is not a matter of priority to the government, and I have been urging the Prime Minister to give us some positive, constructive proposals with respect to the problem, rather than indulging in rhetoric from one part of the country to the other. 1 pointed this out on an earlier occasion, but the Prime Minister has not yet made any speech on the matter of national unity in the House of Commons.
I suggest that this is the place for the Prime Minister to debate, with other elected representatives from across Canada, his proposals, if he has any, to keep the country together. I suggest that he should not be creating new bureaucracies every time he opens his mouth in an effort to recycle Jean-Luc Pepin, a defeated Liberal cabinet minister, who is all of a sudden to be elevated to the capacity of giving leadership, when we know he will be nothing more than an adjunct to the Liberal Party of Canada. I think it is disgraceful for the Prime Minister, at a time of great difficulty in our country, to contemplate bringing forward a defeated Liberal cabinet minister and to give him a function as an adjunct to the Prime Minister's office, a high profile function, at the expense of the Canadian people. We know Mr. Pepin is nothing more than a political arm of the Prime Minister and of the Liberal party.
There have been no definitions of the roles of the bureaucracies which have been created. What does the federal-provincial relations office do? On Friday we referred to a speech by Mr. Gordon Robertson who, during the life of this government under our present Prime Minister, has been in charge of the federal-provincial relations office. I got the impression that in the speech he made last week there was an attempt to get back
May 16, 1977

into the dialogue, yet the content of his speech was rejected and repudiated by the Acting Prime Minister, who said Mr. Robertson did not state government policy in anything he said in those remarks. This man is clearly involved with federal-provincial relations. Apparently he has been in charge of that whole process for the last six or seven years. Now apparently he is being phased out by the creation of the Tellier bureaucracy within the Prime Minister's office and the Privy Council office, which is involved in the development of policies and studies with respect to Quebec, and now we hear that there is a possibility of a new national unity commission.
I was amused at a Canadian Press interview with Mr. Pepin which was reported in part in the Ottawa Citizen of April 30, 1977, as follows:
"Too many people think that to work for national unity you have to specialize in constitutional law."
The position as head of a high-profile national unity commission has been the one most often linked to him in recent days. But he confesses the idea worries him somewhat.
In an article in the Ottawa Citizen of April 30 John Gray writes that Mr. Pepin said the Prime Minister wanted him to do for national unity much the same job as he has done at the Anti-Inflation Board for the fight against inflation. I can only suggest that if that is the case we are in serious difficulty indeed.

Mr. Speaker, I am rather intrigued by the newly discovered interest of my hon. friend and his Conservative colleagues in national unity. Their sudden recognition of the significance of issues affecting Confederation and Canadian unity is revealing in its timing. It smacks more of expediency than substance or conviction.
I am also intrigued by the new role my hon. friend has assumed in recent months in the House of Commons. I did not notice this role in his early days in the Chamber when he and I were freshmen here. The role he has assumed in recent weeks is reflected to a certain extent in his remarks tonight and on other occasions. I seems to be that of a hatchetman, either with respect to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or Mr. Pepin, or whomsoever is under discussion at any given moment. It used to be that he could be counted upon for positive and constructive contributions, but unfortunately that seems to be lacking recently.
With respect to the specific point raised during question period last Friday and repeated tonight, it should be emphasized that the notion of a so-called "third unity organization or bureaucracy" is a product of the hon. member's own question, or perhaps some misinterpretation that may have been reported in the press. There is nothing that I can find in Hansard to indicate that that is a government suggestion. Neither is there anything to be found in the transcript of the Prime Minister's news conference of April 28 to substantiate the point alleged
Adjournment Debate
tonight. During that news conference Mr. Pepin's position was discussed.
The Prime Minister indicated that Mr. Pepin is a distinguished Canadian who has made a tremendous contribution to the country for many years in many ways. It is obvious that the government, the Prime Minister, and I think Canadians generally, would value his continued participation in the federal arena. As the Prime Minister has indicated, some discussions have taken place, but there are no conclusions to report yet. I, for one, hope that Mr. Pepin will continue doing what he has done so well for so many years, that is, to keep on working very hard for Canada.

subtopic: ENERGY-PROPOSED UPGRADING FACILITY FOR HEAVY OIL AT LLOYDMINSTER-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON FEASIBILITY REPORT
ENERGY-PROPOSED UPGRADING FACILITY FOR HEAVY OIL AT LLOYDMINSTER-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON FEASIBILITY REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my purpose in rising this evening is to obtain some elaboration on the question I posed to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) on April 28 with respect to questions about the announcement of a consortium of 20 major oil companies to engage in the establishment of an upgrading facility for heavy oil in the Lloydminster region and the fact that an initial feasibility study had been submitted to the minister for consideration.
My purpose in questioning the minister on April 28 was to determine if his officials had an opportunity to examine the feasibility study and to report to the House what action the federal government has taken. In my view the minister was vague in his answer.
On May 9 a CP news story in the Edmonton Journal advised that new oil sands tax incentives were coming. It reported that the oil industry may soon get a look at new proposals for provincial and federal government royalties and taxes for oil sands. The news story said that the minister had made this remark in addressing the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works.
My purpose in posing the question was to try to ascertain what action had been taken. The minister somewhat deviated from the question by talking about a tar sands plant in the Fort McMurray region, and did not deal with the question of the heavy oil upgrading facility in any detail. As interested Canadians we are all concerned about the challenge of meeting our energy requirements. Day in and day out we see a greater importance placed upon the reserves and the heavy oil deposits in the Lloydminster region, and in the Wainwright and Kinsella areas of Alberta. The Ottawa Citizen of Wednesday, April 27, said in a headline, "Up to 16 billion barrels buried in Canadian fields. Lloydminster's vast belt of heavy crude may help to solve our energy problems." The article reads in part:
The heavy-oil deposits could make a significant contribution to Canada's energy requirements in future, but technological and marketing problems must be overcome,
A recent federal report... says the Lloydminster-type heavy oils are possibly Canada's best hope for expanding oil production in the next 10 to 15 years.

May 16, 1977
Adjournment Debate
A headline in the Edmonton Journal of March 5, 1977, speaks of Lloydminster oil as being a key target. According to the article a heavy oil plant is being proposed. A tremendous amount of interest is being shown in this resource. I think the minister has failed to give a clear answer to the proposal advanced by the consortium of 20 companies for the establishment of a heavy oil upgrading facility. The proposal was submitted to the minister on January 31, 1977. Time is running out, Mr. Speaker. If this facility is to be in place by 1980, we need to know the ground rules, and some important issues ought to have been clarified by the end of the first quarter of 1977. That first quarter is behind us, and time marches on.
I point out that we are considering an important question. We cannot use this particular resource unless it is upgraded. The producers have indicated their interest and desire to spend risk capital on developing this important resource. They propose to establish a 100,000-barrels-a-day oil upgrading facility, modular in design to allow for future expansion. It is estimated that the facility will cost between $500 million and $700 million. It will be located in that particular area; the Hardisty terminal is close by. Further, there is every assurance that the current supply of 100,000 barrels per day of crude is available for the establishment of a viable and feasible facility.
The resources are there. We need the energy, but the major obstacle is that under existing royalty and tax structures, the project is not economically feasible, which means it is not feasible unless there is some modification. That point is the gist of the feasibility study which has been presented to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Basically, it contains two provisions. First, the government of Alberta will have to permit a processing allowance similar to that available with respect to natural gas, to be deducted from the value of the upgraded product. Second, the Government of Canada and the government of Alberta should jointly agree upon an increased capital cost allowance for the project. This is vital, since only with such a measure can the original investment and interest be paid back within seven or eight years after start up, this pay-back period being the condition to be agreed to before the project can be financed.
One may ask, what will be the ultimate cost to the taxpayers of Canada? If all the 100,000 barrels a day of heavy oil feedstock could be marketed without upgrading, the loss in taxes and royalties due to modifications made for the upgrading facility would be in the order of $546 million for Alberta and $399 million for the federal government, over 20 years. However, the proposed 100,000 barrels a day of heavy oil cannot be marketed without upgrading. In fact, more of the supply which would be directed to the upgrading facility would be diverted from other use, the result being not a loss in royalties and taxes, but a substantial gain-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ENERGY-PROPOSED UPGRADING FACILITY FOR HEAVY OIL AT LLOYDMINSTER-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON FEASIBILITY REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the presentation of the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) and the fact that he did not make reference to the Quebec situation. Out of three opposition speakers on the "Late Show", he is the only one who did not mention the situation in Quebec. That is not my favourite subject. I am not obsessed by the situation in Quebec. I have not panicked yet, and I won't. I have heard so many experts on the Quebec situation in the past few days that I do not know if I am qualified to speak about it. In fact, I only reside in Quebec two or three days a week.
The province of Saskatchewan has important heavy oil resources. Currently, heavy crude petroleum represents about 70 per cent of the province's current productive capacity. Heavy crudes have been difficult to market in the past, hence the current interest in upgrading activity which would improve the marketability of the province's oil resources.
Upgrading heavy crudes removes the two main undesirable characteristics, namely, the low gravity and high sulphur. Once this is done the oil will be able to gain wider access to the domestic market. The present reliance on the seasonal demand of the asphalt market will be removed. Canadians will be provided with an additional source of crude supply to help meet the goal of self-reliance.
With these objectives and advantages in mind, there are at present at least two proposals for upgrading operations. Pacific Petroleums, with its partners, has proposed a 100,000 barrel a day facility to be located at Hardisty, Alberta. Husky Oil Limited has proposed a 50,000 barrel a day facility to be located at Lloydminster. Both proposals are in preliminary stages of discussion and examination of projected economics. Other proposals have also been raised. Preliminary economic evaluation work indicates that the economics are marginal at best based on current pricing. The cost estimates for a facility are in the order of hundreds of millions of dollars with no certainty in the present upgrading technology. Consequently the undertaking of an upgrading facility by either industry or government carries a considerable degree of risk.
The government is pleased with the initiative being taken by the various companies which are pursuing the upgrading option for development of our heavy crude oil resources. Officials are keeping in close touch with the companies on the various problems associated with this resource development. There are important questions of technology and crude oil price differentials involved, as well as fiscal arrangements, both federal and provincial, to be worked out for these multimillion dollar projects.
